items.prompt: Explain why the primary sector's share of national output tends to fall as a country's income per head rises.
items.canonical_answer: Three forces push in the same direction. Mechanisation raises the output each worker produces, so the same tonnage of ore or grain needs fewer people and a smaller share of the country's resources. Reserves of a mineral are depleted, so what is left costs more to extract and less is worth extracting. And households with more income spend proportionally less of it on food and raw materials and more on services, so demand grows faster elsewhere. Because the measure is a share, the primary sector's proportion can fall while its output is still rising.
marking_guidance: Reason: at least one of the three forces must be developed rather than named.
The answer must say why the share moves, and should note that a falling share is not the same as falling output.

items.prompt: Explain the mechanism by which a manufacturer contracting out its cleaning and logistics moves activity from the secondary sector to the tertiary sector.
items.canonical_answer: The work itself does not change; who is employed to do it does. While the cleaners and drivers are on the manufacturer's payroll their output is counted inside a manufacturing business, so it falls in the secondary sector. When the manufacturer signs a contract with a cleaning company and a haulier instead, the same hours are now produced by service businesses and are counted in the tertiary sector, and the manufacturer buys them in as a service. The measured share of the secondary sector therefore falls and the tertiary share rises without anybody producing anything new, which is one reason sector shares move faster than the underlying activity does.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: the answer must explain how the activity is reclassified because the employer changes, not merely assert that outsourcing grows the service sector.

items.prompt: Analyse the effects on a mining town of a sustained fall in the relative importance of the primary sector.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition: the town's employment is concentrated in extraction and in the businesses that supply it. As the sector's share of output falls, mines cut shifts or close, so mining employment in the town falls first. The mechanism that spreads it is spending: wages that were spent in local shops, workshops and transport businesses are no longer earned, so those businesses lose revenue and cut their own staff, and the loss reaches households that never worked in mining. items.prompt: Explain what it means to say that an incorporated business is a separate legal person.
items.canonical_answer: It means the business exists in law as something distinct from the people who own it. It owns assets in its own name rather than in theirs, it makes its own contracts, it can sue and be sued as itself, and it continues to exist when a member sells out or dies. Two consequences follow directly: the debts belong to the business rather than to the owners, which is where limited liability comes from, and the business has a continuous existence that does not depend on any one person.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between an unincorporated business and an incorporated business.
items.canonical_answer: Both are businesses owned by people who supply capital and take the returns. The difference is legal identity. An unincorporated business - a sole trader or an ordinary partnership - has no identity separate from its owners, so the owners contract personally, carry unlimited liability for the debts, and the business ends in law when they leave it. An incorporated business - a private or public limited company - is a separate legal person that owns assets and contracts in its own name, gives its members limited liability, and continues when a member sells out or dies. Nearly every other difference between the forms, including which can issue shares, follows from which side of this line the business is on.
marking_guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: the difference is whether the business has a legal identity separate from its owners, and the consequence is the treatment of debts, continuity and shares.

items.prompt: Analyse how having no separate legal identity limits what a growing unincorporated business can do.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition: the business and its owners are the same person in law. The first restriction is on capital. There are no shares, because there is no separate person to own them, so new money has to come from the owners' own resources, from retained profit or from borrowing. As the business grows, the amount it needs rises faster than the owners' personal resources do, and borrowing is assessed against those same personal resources, so the ceiling is reached. The second restriction works through risk. Because liability is unlimited, every contract the growing business signs exposes the owners' houses and savings, so the rational response is to turn down large contracts - which caps growth from the demand side as well. The third is continuity: a business that ends in law with its owner is harder to sell as a going concern and harder to hand on, so the owners cannot realise what they have built. The consequence for the business is that growth stalls at the point where the capital it needs and the risk it carries both exceed what individual owners can personally support, which is the usual reason a successful unincorporated business incorporates.

items.prompt: Evaluate the view that the choice between the main types of business ownership is essentially a decision about how much capital a business can raise.
items.canonical_answer:
The view is too narrow, although it captures the most visible difference. Capital access does separate the forms sharply: an unincorporated business has no shares to sell, a private limited company can issue them to people it chooses, and a public limited company can offer them to the general public, which is the largest single step in the topic. For a business whose binding constraint is money, this is the decision.

It is not the whole decision, because the forms differ on three other things that bind different businesses. Liability decides how much of an owner's personal wealth is at risk, and for a builder signing contracts worth several times the value of the business, that is the factor that decides the form regardless of capital need. Continuity decides whether the business can be sold or inherited as a going concern. And control decides who can be outvoted, which is why family firms stay private when they could raise more by floating.

The decisive criterion is which constraint actually binds this business. Capital dominates where a specific investment cannot otherwise be funded; liability dominates where the owner's exposure is large relative to their wealth; control dominates where the owners' objective is independence rather than size. The strongest argument for the view is that capital is often the constraint that forces the question in the first place, since a business that needs no more money rarely changes form. The judgement therefore stands only conditionally: the view is right for a business at a funding ceiling, and wrong for an owner whose real problem is personal exposure or who would refuse outside money at any price.

items.prompt: Analyse how the one-member-one-vote rule limits a co-operative's ability to raise capital.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition: votes attach to membership, not to money, and surplus is shared according to use rather than capital contributed. The mechanism runs through what an investor receives. There is therefore no way to reward capital with either control or a proportional return, so outside investors have little reason to supply it and members have little reason to contribute more than the minimum. The consequence is that growth is financed mainly from retained surplus and borrowing, which are both slow, so a co-operative facing an opportunity that needs a large sum quickly - a processing plant, a cold chain - is likely to be unable to take it. The stakeholders who bear that are the members themselves, who keep control at the cost of a slower-growing business, which is the trade the form makes.

items.prompt: Analyse how limited liability increases the amount of capital available to new and risky ventures.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition: an investor deciding whether to put money into a venture is weighing a possible gain against a possible loss, and the size of the possible loss is part of the calculation. Under unlimited liability that loss is unbounded - it includes everything the investor owns - so a rational investor will only put money into ventures they can supervise closely enough to control the risk, which in practice means their own business. Investors can put small amounts into many ventures, because each loss is bounded, and they can invest in businesses run by people they do not know and cannot supervise, because no amount of mismanagement can reach beyond the sum committed. The consequence is that savings which would otherwise stay in property or deposits are available to businesses, and new ventures - which are the ones most likely to fail and therefore the ones an unbounded loss would most deter - can raise money from strangers. The stakeholders who gain are entrepreneurs with ideas and no capital, and the economy through the ventures that would not otherwise start.

items.prompt: Evaluate the view that limited liability is unfair to the suppliers and lenders of a small company.
items.canonical_answer:
There is something in the view, but it describes a risk that is disclosed and priced rather than an unfairness. The complaint is real in its mechanism: a supplier delivering goods on thirty days' credit to a small company has a claim that stops at the company's assets, so if the company fails the supplier absorbs the loss while the shareholders lose only what they put in - which in a company formed with minimal share capital may be very little. The people who did the work or supplied the goods carry a risk the owners have contracted out of.

What weakens the view is that the arrangement is public and the other side can act on it. The company's status is on its name and on the public register, its accounts are filed, and a supplier or lender who chooses to extend credit to it does so knowing where the claim stops. They respond accordingly: banks take security or personal guarantees from the directors, suppliers ask for payment in advance until a record exists, and both charge more where the risk is higher. A creditor who does none of these has accepted the risk at a price.

The decisive consideration is what the alternative would produce. Without limited liability, far less capital would reach small and new businesses, because investors would face unbounded loss in ventures they cannot supervise - and the suppliers complaining about the rule would have fewer customers to supply. The judgement is therefore that the rule is defensible but not costless, and it depends on the protections working: where a company is formed with almost no capital specifically so that its debts can be walked away from, the complaint becomes fair, which is why company law provides for directors to be held personally responsible in those cases.

items.prompt: Frans has traded as a sole trader for nine years installing solar systems. He now employs six people, holds N$900 000 of stock on credit from a single supplier, and has been offered a contract to fit systems at forty schools, worth N$11 million over two years, with payment ninety days after each installation is certified. He owns a house worth about N$2.3 million. His bank has said it would advance working capital against the contract but would want personal security. Analyse the liability position Frans is in, and evaluate what he should do before signing the contract.
items.canonical_answer:
The position first. As a sole trader Frans and his business are the same person in law, so every obligation is his personally and without limit: the N$900 000 owed to his supplier, the wages of six employees, and anything that goes wrong on forty roofs. The contract makes this materially worse in a way the headline figure hides. Ninety-day payment terms mean he must fund materials and labour for each installation for three months before he is paid, and across forty schools the peak amount he has outstanding will be a large fraction of N$11 million - money owed to his supplier and his staff while the schools have not yet paid. Against that exposure he owns a house worth N$2.3 million and nothing else substantial.

Incorporating would move those obligations onto a company, so a failure by the schools to pay, or a defect claim on an installation, would stop at the company's assets. Two things limit how much that helps. The bank has already said it wants personal security, so the working capital facility would be guaranteed by Frans whatever form he trades in, and that protection is given up for that debt. And his supplier, faced with a newly incorporated company, may ask for a guarantee too or shorten his credit terms, which would worsen the cash position the contract creates.

Recommendation: incorporate before signing, and negotiate the payment terms rather than relying on the legal form to carry the risk. The decisive factor is the mismatch between ninety-day payment and immediate cost, because that is what turns a profitable contract into an obligation larger than everything he owns. Incorporation is worth doing because it caps the claims he has not guaranteed - the supplier balance, employment claims, installation defects - and those are the ones most likely to arise. The strongest argument against doing it now is that his supplier relationship, built over nine years, rests on his personal standing and may be repriced when the counterparty becomes a company. That is why the recommendation is conditional on two things: agreeing staged payment or a deposit with the schools so the outstanding amount never approaches the value of the business, and agreeing continued terms with the supplier in writing before the change. If neither can be obtained, he should take the contract in phases - ten schools at a time - rather than signing for forty.

items.prompt: Forty women in the Kunene region harvest and press marula oil. At present each sells to traders who call at the village. A development agency has offered to fund a press and a store, and asks them to choose between forming a producer co-operative owned by the forty, and forming a social enterprise run by a small board that would buy their fruit at a guaranteed price and reinvest its surplus in the community. Analyse the difference between the two options for these women, and evaluate which they should choose.
items.canonical_answer:
The two options differ on who owns the business and therefore on who takes the risk and the reward. In the co-operative the forty are the owners. They control it one member one vote, the surplus is shared according to how much oil each sold through it, and the value of the press and the store belongs to them. In the social enterprise they are suppliers rather than owners: they receive a guaranteed price for fruit, which removes their exposure to a bad year, but the surplus goes to the board's chosen community purposes and the assets are not theirs.

For these particular women three facts decide how that difference plays out. They are forty, which is large enough for one-member-one-vote decision-making to be slow and small enough for everyone to know each other. They currently sell to whoever calls, so their problem is bargaining power and a price they do not set. And the capital is coming from an agency rather than from them, which means the co-operative's usual weakness - members supplying capital that buys no extra say - does not bite at the start, though it will bite when the press needs replacing.

Recommendation: the co-operative. The decisive criterion is that their central problem is control over price, and only the co-operative gives them that permanently: as owners they decide what to charge buyers and what to pay themselves, and the surplus returns to them in proportion to what they contributed. The guaranteed price in the social enterprise solves the same problem for as long as the board chooses to maintain it, and they would have no vote if it did not. The strongest argument the other way is capability: a small board can hire a manager, negotiate with exporters and reinvest without convening forty people, and a co-operative that cannot make decisions will lose the season. That is why the recommendation is conditional on two things - a written rule delegating day-to-day trading decisions to an elected committee of three or four, and paid management brought in from outside if nobody among the forty can do it. If the agency will not fund management alongside the press, the social enterprise becomes the safer choice, because a guaranteed price from a functioning business is worth more than ownership of one that cannot trade.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a recommendation is required.
Context: the analysis must use the women's facts - forty members, selling to traders who call, agency-funded capital.
Criterion: the decisive factor is which option gives them lasting control over the price they receive.
Counterargument: must address the co-operative's decision-making and management weakness.
Condition: must state what the recommendation depends on and what would reverse it.

items.prompt: A country's sector shares of employment over twenty years are: primary 34% to 19%, secondary 21% to 18%, tertiary and quaternary together 45% to 63%. Identify what has happened to the relative importance of each sector, explain two reasons for the change, and explain one consequence for the people who worked in the declining sector.
items.canonical_answer:
The primary sector has fallen sharply in relative importance, from just over a third of employment to under a fifth. The secondary sector has fallen slightly, by three percentage points. The tertiary and quaternary sectors together have risen from under half to almost two thirds, and are now the great majority of employment.

Two reasons. First, mechanisation in the primary sector: machinery raises the output each worker produces, so the same tonnage of crops or ore needs fewer people, and employment falls even where output does not. Second, rising incomes: households with more income spend proportionally more of it on services - travel, health care, finance, entertainment - so demand and therefore employment grow fastest in the tertiary sector.

One consequence for the people released by the primary sector is structural unemployment. Their skills were specific to extraction or to farm work and do not transfer to the service jobs that are growing, and those jobs are usually in towns rather than in the districts where the primary work was. So vacancies and unemployment can exist side by side: the jobs are real but the people released cannot take them without retraining and relocation, both of which take years.

Note that these are employment shares, so they show where people work rather than what each sector produced; primary output may have risen over the same period.
marking_guidance: Each part must be answered: identify the direction for each sector as a point, give two reasons, and give one consequence.
The reason for each change must be explained rather than named, because a list of causes without a mechanism does not show understanding.
Context: the answer must use the figures given for each sector rather than describing sector change in general.
The point that these are shares of employment, not of output, should be made.
